snippet.title: The Solar Breakthrough That Could Change Everything
snippet.description:
For over 50 years, silicon has powered the solar revolution.

But there’s a problem.

Silicon solar panels are approaching their physical efficiency limit — and the world’s energy demand is still rising fast.

Now, a company called Oxford PV may have found the breakthrough that changes everything.

Using a revolutionary material called perovskite, they’ve created the world’s first commercial tandem solar panels — capable of capturing far more energy from sunlight than traditional silicon ever could.

This video explores:
• Why silicon solar panels are reaching their limit
• The science behind perovskite tandem cells
• How Oxford PV commercialized the technology
• Why this could reshape the global energy industry
• The challenges still facing perovskite solar
• And what happens if solar energy becomes truly abundant

If Oxford PV succeeds, this may become one of the most important energy breakthroughs of the century.

Because this isn’t just better solar.

It’s the beginning of a new energy era.

snippet.title: The Scottish Startup Reinventing Wind Turbines
snippet.description:
This unusual wind turbine does not use one giant rotor. Instead, it uses multiple smaller rotors mounted on a modular support structure.

In this video, we break down the Myriad Turbine, developed by Scottish startup Myriad Wind Energy Systems, and look at why this multi-rotor design could become important for distributed wind energy.

We explore how the technology works, why smaller standardised rotors may reduce transport and installation challenges, how the system is designed for redundancy, and why the company believes it could improve cost-effectiveness for on-site wind generation.

We also look at the current development stage, including Myriad’s 2 kW 4-rotor proof-of-concept demonstrator installed in Scotland in April 2024, and the company’s longer-term concept for larger modular wind turbines.

This is not yet a fully commercial mass-market turbine, and the final price has not been publicly fixed. But the design is a serious attempt to solve real wind energy problems: transport, maintenance, site access, material cost, and local renewable power generation.

Could the future of some wind turbines be many smaller rotors working together instead of one giant rotor?

Watch to find out.

Multi-rotor wind turbine design
Modular wind turbine technology
Distributed wind energy
Small wind power
Wind turbine transport and installation
On-site renewable energy

Artificial intelligence may feel digital, weightless, and hidden somewhere in “the cloud.” But behind every AI prompt, generated image, video, and conversation is something very physical: electricity.

A facility demanding up to 9 gigawatts of power would rival the electricity needs of entire regions. That raises a major question: where will all that energy come from?

This is not just a data center story.
It is an energy story.
A pipeline story.
A grid story.
And possibly one of the defining infrastructure battles of the AI era.

snippet.title: Did I Get the Wrong Heat Pump: Geothermal vs Air Source
snippet.description:
Geothermal vs Air Source Heat Pump: Which is Worth It? What if the most efficient way to heat and cool your home might not actually be the best choice for you? Geothermal heat pumps are the gold standard for efficiency. They're also the most expensive upfront investment you can make in your home's HVAC system. So, are they really worth it? Or should you go with an air source heat pump instead? I've been living with my geothermal system for two years now. I reached out to my friend Paul Braren, who installed an air source heat pump system in his home around the same time I was building mine. We're both in New England, we both have detailed energy monitoring, and we both ditched fossil fuels completely. It’s the perfect setup for a real-world comparison. Here's the thing, though. After crunching the numbers, this isn't going to be the straightforward "geothermal wins" or "air source is better" story you might expect. The actual data surprised both of us.

snippet.description:
In this short video the professor Neildeegrasstayson explains why there will be never glying cars.

Neil deGrasse Tyson (US: /dəˈɡræs/ də-GRASS or UK: /dəˈɡrɑːs/ də-GRAHSS; born October 5, 1958) is an American astrophysicist, author, and science communicator. Tyson studied at Harvard University, the University of Texas at Austin, and Columbia University. From 1991 to 1994, he was a postdoctoral research associate at Princeton University. In 1994, he joined the Hayden Planetarium as a staff scientist and the Princeton faculty as a visiting research scientist and lecturer. In 1996, he became director of the planetarium and oversaw its $210 million reconstruction project, which was completed in 2000. Since 1996, he has been the director of the Hayden Planetarium at the Rose Center for Earth and Space in New York City. The center is part of the American Museum of Natural History, where Tyson founded the Department of Astrophysics in 1997 and has been a research associate in the department since 2003…
